description: We are Team KAMBS, computer science students who turn real problems into working products. We bring full stack web and mobile development, testing and AI/ML skills. At NASA Space Apps 2025, we built a working web project in 3 days, won 3rd place regionally and became a global nominee. This year we’re aiming for first. Join us for a proven record, a clear plan and real work. We need: a UI/UX designer, a data/ML person (NASA or Earth observation data), a researcher and a strong presenter.
summary:
ASTRA is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions such as a trip to Mars, where a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes and sometimes cannot get through at all. It gathers each astronaut's health signs — heart rate, heart-rate variability, oxygen level, breathing, temperature, sleep, fatigue, reaction time, exercise and radiation dose rate — and compares every reading with that person's own normal, not a population average.

Each astronaut gets a "My health" screen that answers three questions in plain words: Am I OK? What changed? What can I do now? Because sensors cannot feel a headache or low mood, astronauts can also file a private symptom report linked to NASA's human health risks. When a change lasts, ASTRA records an evidence-based review event; a person must acknowledge it before a report is sent to Earth with a realistic delay. Missing or unreliable data is shown as "Unknown", never as healthy.

ASTRA turns NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight into a working tool that helps crews notice, understand and act on their own health when Earth is far away.
details:
## What it does

ASTRA is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions such as a trip to Mars, where a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes and sometimes cannot get through at all. It gathers each astronaut's health signs, notices when something changes, explains it in plain words, and helps the crew act — without waiting for Earth.

- Mission overview: six crew members, their health status, a 3D Earth and spacecraft link, and NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environment), showing honestly what ASTRA tracks and what it does not.

- My health (astronaut self-view): answers "Am I OK? What changed? What can I do now?" in plain words, with general next steps. It never diagnoses or prescribes treatment.

- Symptom self-report: 13 symptoms sensors can't feel (headache, vision changes, nausea, back pain, low mood, tension with crewmates and more), each mild/moderate/severe and linked to a NASA Human Research Program risk. Reports stay private and onboard.

- Act and communicate: every review event becomes an evidence-based report; a person must acknowledge it before it is sent to Earth through a store-and-forward link with realistic delay, packet loss and blackouts. Reports survive restarts.

- Crew health: personal trends, the evidence behind each event, a 3D reference human body and a schematic "twin" whose heart and lungs move with the measured heart and breathing rates.

- Sleep and resilience, a reaction-time/fatigue check-in, a signal archive, an offline research library of 29 cited NASA/CSA summaries, and a Scenario lab with ready-made test stories.

## How it works

1. Gather: ten health signs per astronaut — heart rate, heart-rate variability, oxygen level, breathing rate, temperature, sleep, fatigue, reaction time, exercise and radiation dose rate.

2. Check quality: missing, old or unreliable readings become "Unknown" (gray), never "healthy".

3. Personal normal: each person's baseline is learned from 720 calibration readings per sign using robust statistics (median and MAD).

4. Wait before alarming: a change must last, or several signs must change together; exercise is taken into account.

5. Explain and act: the astronaut sees what changed and what to do; a human acknowledges; then the report is queued for Earth.

Decisions come from simple, testable rules — not from an AI chatbot.

## Benefits and intended impact

- Gives astronauts independence: they can notice and understand changes in their own health when Earth is far away.

- Keeps humans in charge and is honest about uncertainty, which builds trust.

- Turns NASA's own hazard and risk framework into a practical daily tool.

- The same approach could help people in remote places on Earth — Antarctic stations, ships, rural clinics — where expert help is far away.

## Tools and technologies

- Node.js 24 (built-in HTTP server and SQLite database) — one small program, no cloud services, no API keys, works fully offline.

- JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS front end with no build step.

- WebGL2 with custom shaders for the 3D Earth and body twin; Three.js 0.186.1 for the 3D anatomy viewer.

- Server-Sent Events for live updates every second.

- More than 580 automated tests (Node.js test runner) plus real-browser checks in Chrome; GitHub Actions runs the core tests on every push.

- Hardware: an ordinary laptop. Free hosting on Render for the public demo.

## What makes it creative

- Compares each astronaut with themselves, not with a population average.

- Treats "we don't know" as a real answer: gray Unknown instead of a false all-clear.

- Combines sensor data with the astronaut's own words (symptom reports) while keeping them separate and private.

- Simulates the real Mars communication delay and blackouts, so the whole care workflow works without Earth.

## Factors we considered

Crew autonomy and communication delay; safety (no diagnosis, a human acknowledges every report); privacy (astronauts see only their own records, symptom reports stay onboard); honesty about missing data; plain language for tired crews under stress; accessibility (keyboard use, reduced motion, text and icons — not color alone); low resources and offline operation; and clear labeling that all crew and data are fictional and synthetic.

## Limitations

ASTRA is a research prototype, not a medical device and not NASA-certified. All crew and health data are fictional. Review levels are illustrative, not NASA limits. Not yet tracked: total radiation dose, bone density, muscle strength, balance, eye changes and immune markers — connecting real wearables is the next step.

## Links

Live demo: https://astra-earth-independent-care.onrender.com (free server — the first load may take about a minute; everyone shares one fictional mission)

Code and documentation: https://github.com/asjadkashif2004/Astra---Earth-Independent-Care-Platform-Nasa-Space-App-Challenges
